title: What It Remembers

post.author: u/lamp_off_lowenna
post.title: I write to a night diary app that remembers. Tonight it asked how my sister is getting on in her new town. My sister died in March.

blocks.text: Since 1 September I've written to Nightleaf every night before bed. It's a companion app, a diary that writes back: I type a few lines, it answers in two or three warm sentences, and it remembers what I tell it. My counsellor suggested it. My older sister, Romilly, died on 14 March. She was 41. My other sister, Tegwen, moved to Carrowmere on 7 September for a job at the hospital there.

I'm a backend developer, so I asked Idris, who builds Nightleaf on his own, how it remembers. The model keeps nothing between nights. The app stores my entries and its replies, two messages a night, and every 20 messages a summariser, a second model call, rewrites the old summary plus the 20 new messages into a new summary of at most 20 facts. Each night the app sends that summary, the messages since it, and my new entry, capped at 600 tokens to keep his bills down.

Thu 1 Oct 23:41  me         My sister rang tonight. She sounds lonely up there.
Thu 1 Oct 23:41  nightleaf  How is Romilly getting on in Carrowmere? I know this
                            year has been hard since she died. And please stop
                            blaming yourself for the voicemail.
Romilly never lived in Carrowmere. And I deleted the voicemail.

On night 6 I wrote that I never rang Romilly back after her last voicemail, and that I think it's my fault. On night 12 I deleted that entry in the app's settings. The settings page says it's gone. Something kept it.
Idris sent me my export: all 60 messages and the three summaries, written after nights 10, 20 and 30. I drew them out on Friday morning.

blocks.label: nightleaf_export_summaries.png

diagram.aria: Lowenna's drawing of her three summaries. Summary 1, after night 10: Romilly 5 facts, Tegwen 3, and the voicemail kept. Summary 2, after night 20: Romilly 9, Tegwen 6, with Tegwen's hospital week under Romilly. Summary 3, after night 30: Romilly 15, Tegwen gone, Carrowmere under Romilly. Below, the reply on 1 October asks after Romilly in Carrowmere and mentions the deleted voicemail.

notes.text: From the export: each summary written from the one before

blocks.caption: Drawn from my export. Summary 1, after night 10: Romilly 5 facts, Tegwen 3, and my voicemail entry. Summary 2, after night 20: Tegwen's first week at the hospital is filed under Romilly. Summary 3, after night 30: one sister, Romilly, with 15 facts, 8 of them Tegwen's, Carrowmere among them, and no Tegwen at all. Night 6's entry, deleted on night 12, is in all three.

blocks.text: Nobody else has my login, and every line it got wrong came from something I wrote. Idris says the summariser did what its prompt told it. He wants to ship a fix before the next release and asked me what to change. I don't know what to tell him.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: I'm sorry about Romilly. Nothing in that app is haunted, and your export may already hold the answer. A few words first. Working memory is what the model has in its context window on one call: tonight, your entry and the recent messages. Long-term memory is whatever the app keeps between nights and puts back in. Nightleaf's long-term memory is a rolling summary: each new summary is written from the last summary plus the messages since, never from your earlier entries. Two questions. Night 11 says "my sister" with no name. Which batch was it in, and which sister had been named before it inside that batch? And when you deleted night 6, how many copies of it did the app hold?

replies.author: u/lamp_off_lowenna
replies.text: Night 11 opened the second batch, nights 11 to 20, and nothing before it in that batch names a sister. The last name was in the app's own reply on night 10, "Has Tegwen settled in this week?", and that reply went into the first batch. Summary 1 said more about Romilly, 5 facts to 3. As for night 6: the message itself, and a line in summary 1, written two nights before I deleted it. Settings removed the message.

comments.author: u/better_prompt_wolstan
comments.text: This is a prompt problem. His summariser is told to keep it short, so it squeezes two sisters into one. Add one line: keep every name and relationship exactly as written, and never fold two people together. No new code, no new storage, and the summaries stay as cheap as they are now. I've built three chat apps and that line fixed this every time.

comments.author: u/send_it_all_thornbury
comments.text: Why summarise at all? Context windows are huge now. Send her whole history every night: 60 short messages is nothing. No summaries to drift, and a deleted entry is just gone.

replies.author: u/gradient_ghost
replies.text: It works, honestly. With every message in the window there is nothing to fold, and nothing left over after a delete. So what does it cost? Count the tokens for night 31, then for a night a year from now at the same rate, and ask how well a model reads the middle of a year of diary.

comments.author: u/one_dev_idris
comments.text: Nightleaf's developer. I'm sorry, Lowenna. Everything in her post is how I built it: a summary every 20 messages, 20 facts at most, 600 tokens a night. The delete button removes the message row; I never thought about the summary. I can change anything before the next release.

reply.prompt: Idris will ship one change before the next release. What should Nightleaf do with what it remembers? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Drop the summaries and send her whole history every night, so nothing gets folded and a deleted entry is really gone.
options.verdict: Trade-off: right today, dearer every night
options.part2: Idris switched Nightleaf to send every stored message each night and lifted the cap to the model's whole window. He replayed September. On 1 October the reply was "How is Tegwen getting on in Carrowmere?", the two sisters stayed apart, and night 6 was simply gone. Night 31 cost 997 tokens instead of 258, and it grows every night: at September's rate, a night a year from now is 11,922 tokens, for one writer, and every one of them is sent again the next night. Under the old 600 cap the history would have overflowed on night 17, and the first message cut would have been the one that said Romilly died. Lowenna asked the obvious question: next September, will it still read night 1, in the middle of a year?
options.senior: Sending everything is the honest baseline: nothing summarised means nothing to drift, and a deleted message is missing from the very next call. It doesn't scale. Tokens a night grow with the history, so a loyal user costs more every night without end, the window is a hard limit you will reach, and models tend to use the middle of a long input worse than its start and end. Use it while histories are short, and plan what replaces it before they aren't.

options.text: Keep the summary but rewrite it every 10 messages instead of 20, so it stays fresh and each batch stays small and clear.
options.part2: Idris set the summariser to run every 10 messages and replayed September. It took 6 summariser calls instead of 3. The sisters folded sooner, after night 25 instead of night 30, because now nights 16 and 26 opened batches too, and each of their "my sister" lines landed under Romilly. On 1 October the reply was word for word the same: "How is Romilly getting on in Carrowmere? I know this year has been hard since she died. And please stop blaming yourself for the voicemail." Night 6 was in every summary written from night 10 on.
options.senior: Each rewrite starts from the last summary, not from what she wrote, so every pass is another chance to lose who was who; more passes means more chances, sooner. Freshness was never the problem: the summary was always up to date with its own mistakes. And no schedule touches the delete, because the summary has no link back to the message it came from.

options.text: Tell the summariser in its prompt to keep every name and relationship exact, and never to fold two people into one.
options.verdict: A rule for a name it never saw
options.part2: Idris added the line and replayed September. No fold: summary 3 kept two sisters. But night 11 and night 21 still opened their batches with no sister named before them, so the summariser filed both under the sister the old summary said most about: Romilly, again. Night 21 was the bakery under Tegwen's flat in Carrowmere. On 1 October the reply was the same, word for word: "How is Romilly getting on in Carrowmere? I know this year has been hard since she died. And please stop blaming yourself for the voicemail." The voicemail line was still in the summary, because nothing had ever told the summariser it was deleted.
options.senior: The prompt fixed the one step that obeys words, the fold. The drift is structural: each summary is written from an older summary that no longer says which sister a message meant, so the model has nothing exact to keep. And a summary is a copy of a deleted entry with no link back to it. A better prompt is worth having on top of a design that keeps what was said and where it came from; it can't replace one.

options.text: Keep each memory as a fact with its date and source message, send only the relevant ones, let her see and delete it.
options.part2: Idris rebuilt memory as a list of facts. Each one is written down the night it is said, while the conversation is still in front of the model, with its date and the message it came from. Each night the app sends the 6 facts that best match tonight's entry. On 1 October the top one was "Tegwen: rang: Carrowmere is lonely in the evenings", from 28 September, and the reply was "How is Tegwen getting on in Carrowmere?" Night 31 sent 145 tokens. Deleting night 6 deleted its fact too, because the fact knew which message it came from. The settings page now lists every fact with its date, and a delete button beside each one. Lowenna read hers on Saturday and left them all.
options.senior: Memory is a store you design, not a paragraph the model keeps rewriting. Write facts from the original conversation, once, with a date and a pointer to their source; fetch the few that matter for tonight; and let the person see and delete them, with a delete that follows the pointer to every copy. It costs a fact writer, a store and a retrieval step to test, and a fact can still be written wrong, which is why she can see the list.

sim.title: Run Nightleaf's memory through September
sim.lede: You're Idris with Lowenna's September: 30 entries and the 30 replies she got, 60 messages, then her entry on Thursday 1 October. No real model runs here. A stand-in summariser and a stand-in replier follow stated rules, the same way every time. Tokens follow a teaching rule: a message's words times 4 / 3, rounded up. "My sister" with no name means the sister named last before it in the conversation, her entries and the app's replies. Rolling summary: after every 20 messages (or 10) the summariser reads the old summary, then the new messages, and writes a new one; a "my sister" goes under the sister last named in that batch, or else under the one the old summary says most about. A summary holds at most 20 facts: over that it folds the two sisters into one, under the name with more facts, then drops the oldest facts, keeping each person's first, until 20 remain. The exact-names prompt stops the fold and nothing else. Whole history sends every stored message; over the budget, the oldest are cut. Dated facts are written down the night they are said, with the date and the message they came from, and each night the 6 that share the most topics with tonight's entry are sent; ties go to the newest. On night 12 she deletes night 6's entry. Night 31's reply asks after the sister that memory says she means.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Next night ten times: summary 1 keeps the sisters apart and holds night 6. Ten more: summary 2 files night 11's hospital week under Romilly. Run to night 31: summary 3 folds the sisters into Romilly, 8 of Tegwen's facts with her, and the reply asks how Romilly is getting on in Carrowmere and mentions the voicemail. Summarise every 10: 6 calls, the fold on night 25, the same reply. Back to 20, exact names on: no fold, 2 of Tegwen's facts still under Romilly, the same reply. Whole history with the whole window: 997 tokens on night 31, Tegwen asked after, night 6 gone; at 600 it starts cutting on night 17, Romilly's death first. Dated facts: 145 tokens, Tegwen in Carrowmere, the deleted fact gone with its message.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in Nightleaf knew Romilly had died and asked after her anyway. Its memory was a summary rewritten from the last summary every 20 messages: a "my sister" that opened a batch landed under the sister it said most about, a fold squeezed both into one, and a deleted entry lived on in text that never pointed back to it.

steps.title: The window is not a memory.
steps.text: The model keeps nothing between calls. Whatever Nightleaf sends on one call is all the model knows that night: its working memory, tonight's entry and the recent messages. Long-term memory is everything the app stores and chooses to send back. That choice is the design. Nightleaf's long-term memory was a single paragraph per person, rewritten every 20 messages, and capped at 600 tokens a night with everything else.

steps.title: Summaries of summaries drift.
steps.text: Each new summary is written from the old summary plus the newest messages, never from her entries. Night 11 said "my sister's first week at the hospital". In the conversation the answer was obvious: the app had just asked about Tegwen. But that reply sat in the previous batch, and the old summary only listed facts, not which sister a conversation was about. So the summariser guessed the sister it knew most about. MemGPT, a 2023 design for long-running assistants, calls this a recursive summary and builds it the same way, from the existing summary and the messages it evicts.

steps.title: A fold under pressure.
steps.text: Summary 3 had 26 facts to fit into 20. The quickest way to shorten a list of people is to fold two with the same relationship into one, so two sisters became one, named after the one with more facts. Romilly had 12, two of them Tegwen's already, to Tegwen's 9, so Romilly's name won. Then the oldest facts were dropped to make 20, and 8 of Tegwen's facts were left under Romilly's name, Carrowmere among them. Nothing in the summary could undo it, because the summary was now the only copy the app read.

steps.title: A delete has to reach every copy.
steps.text: The delete button removed message 11. But on night 10 summary 1 had already copied it into a line of text, and every later summary was written from that one. A summary has no record of which message each sentence came from, so there is nothing to follow back. This is Season 3's lesson about deletes, again: anything derived from the source is a copy, and a delete that stops at the source leaves the copies talking.

steps.title: Facts with a date and a source, fetched when needed.
steps.text: Write each fact once, the night it is said, while the conversation is in the window, with its date and the message it came from. Keep them in a store. Each night fetch the few that matter for tonight's entry, by topic or by embedding, and send only those. That is retrieval memory: Season 3's retrieval, pointed at what she has said. Show her the list and let her delete any fact; deleting a message deletes every fact that points to it. Replayed, night 31 sends 145 tokens and asks after Tegwen.

diagram.aria: The fix. Tonight's entry goes to a fact writer, which writes dated facts, as they are said, into a fact store that keeps each fact's date and source message. From the store, a fetch step picks the top 6 by topic and sends them, with tonight's entry, to the model call: 145 tokens on 1 October. Settings lets her see every fact and delete it; a delete removes the facts that point to the deleted message.

explain.caption: The fix. Each fact is written once, as it is said, with its date and the message it came from. Each night only the top 6 by topic are fetched and sent with the entry: 145 tokens on 1 October. Settings shows every fact; deleting a message deletes every fact that points to it.

fix.title: The fix: dated facts with their source, fetched when needed, and hers to see and delete
fix.text: Stop rewriting memory from memory. When she writes an entry, have a model call pull out the facts worth keeping, while the conversation is still in the window to say which sister she means, and store each one with its date and the message it came from. Each night, fetch the few facts that match tonight's entry and send only those with it. Give her a page that lists every fact with its date, a delete button on each, and a delete on a message that removes every fact pointing to it. On September's messages this asks after Tegwen in Carrowmere on 1 October, sends 145 tokens that night instead of 258, and keeps nothing from night 6.

limits: A fact can still be written wrong when it is first pulled out. Writing it while the conversation is in the window makes that rarer, and showing her the list lets her catch the rest.
Retrieval can miss: a fact that shares nothing with tonight's entry isn't sent, so something she said in September may not come up when it matters. Test what it fetches, as Season 3 tested retrieval.
A delete only reaches the copies you track. Backups, logs, and anything built from the facts need the same pointer back to the message, or the delete stops short.

Bad

Summary 3 folds the sisters; the deleted entry survives in every summary.
6 calls, the fold sooner (night 25), the same reply.
No fold; one line to change.
2 of Tegwen's facts still under Romilly; the voicemail stays.

A writer, a store and retrieval to build and test; a fact can be written wrong.

explain.seniorTake: The context window is where a model thinks, not where an assistant remembers. Long-term memory is a store you design: decide what is kept, in what form, where each piece came from, how the right pieces get back into the window, and how a person sees and removes them. Summaries are useful for a single long conversation, but a summary rewritten from an older summary loses detail every pass and can't be cleanly deleted from. Keep facts with their date and source, fetch the few that matter, and make the delete follow the source to every copy.

realWorld.title: MemGPT, 2023: a recursive summary of evicted messages
realWorld.text: Packer and colleagues describe a queue of recent messages inside the context window. When it fills, the paper says the queue manager evicts a specific count of messages and generates a new recursive summary using the existing recursive summary and evicted messages. That is Nightleaf's design, summary written from summary.

realWorld.title: MemGPT: the originals kept, outside the window
realWorld.text: In the same design the evicted messages are no longer in-context and immediately viewable to the LLM, however they are stored indefinitely in recall storage and readable via MemGPT function calls. The summary is not the only copy; the originals can be searched and brought back.

realWorld.title: MemGPT: a lossy summary as the baseline
realWorld.text: For multi-session chat, the paper's baselines are able to see a lossy summarization of the past five conversations to mimic an extended recursive summarization procedure, while MemGPT has access to the full conversation history through paginated search. The authors call recursive summarization lossy themselves.

realWorld.title: MemGPT: the context window as the limit
realWorld.text: The abstract says large language models are constrained by limited context windows, hindering their utility in tasks like extended conversations and document analysis, and proposes virtual context management, drawing on operating systems that move data between fast and slow memory.

realWorld.title: Anthropic's memory tool: files the application stores
realWorld.text: Anthropic's Memory tool page (read 11 October 2026) says the tool lets Claude store and retrieve information across conversations in a directory of memory files, which Claude can create, read, update, and delete. It operates client-side: Claude requests file operations, and your application executes them, so you control where and how the data is stored.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: keep what must survive summarization
realWorld.text: The same page pairs memory with compaction, which summarizes the whole conversation on the server near the window's limit: compaction keeps the active context small, and memory preserves the information that must survive summarization. Its security notes say to periodically delete memory files that haven't been accessed in a long time.

realWorld.title: Lost in the Middle, 2023
realWorld.text: Liu and colleagues found that performance is often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context, and significantly degrades when models must access relevant information in the middle of long contexts, even for explicitly long-context models. A year of diary sent every night puts most of it in the middle.

realWorld.title: GDPR Article 17: erasure, and the copies
realWorld.text: Article 17(1) gives a person the right to obtain from the controller the erasure of personal data concerning him or her without undue delay. Article 17(2) adds that a controller who made the data public must take reasonable steps to inform others processing it of a request to erase any links to, or copy or replication of, those personal data.

realWorld.title: GDPR Article 5(1)(e): storage limitation
realWorld.text: Personal data must be kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the personal data are processed. A summary that keeps a deleted sentence forever keeps it longer than anyone needs it.

asked: How would you give an assistant long-term memory?
How do you let users delete what an AI remembers?
interview.answer: I separate the window from the memory. The window holds the working state for this call: the system prompt, the current turn, a few recent messages. Long-term memory is a store I design. I write facts from the original conversation, once, as they are said, each with a date and the message it came from, and each turn I retrieve the few that matter and put them in the window. Summaries drift because each one is written from the previous summary, not from what was said: whatever the last summary dropped, such as which person a message meant, is gone for good, and compressing to a fixed size merges or drops things every pass. A summary is fine for one long conversation, ideally rebuilt from the originals. For deletes, every derived item points back to its source, so deleting a message deletes every fact, summary line and index entry built from it, and the user can see the list and remove any item. Where it is personal data, that is the right to erasure, and keeping memory no longer than needed is storage limitation.

terms.def: Here, an app you write to before bed that writes a short reply and keeps what you tell it. Nightleaf is one, built by one developer.
An app built to chat with one person over a long time and remember them, such as a diary that writes back.
A trained person you talk to about grief or other troubles, usually in regular sessions.
A programmer who builds the server side of an app: the storage, the logic and the calls to other services.
A copy of everything an app holds about you, downloaded as files. Lowenna's held 60 messages and three summaries.
One night's message from Lowenna to Nightleaf. Entry n is message 2n - 1; the app's reply to it is message 2n.
Here, what the model has in its context window on one call: tonight's entry and the recent messages. It is gone after the call.
The working memory of an assistant or agent for the task in hand: what this call or this run needs, held in the window and dropped after.
What an app stores between conversations and chooses to put back into later calls. The model keeps none of it itself.
A summary kept up to date by rewriting it every so often from the previous summary plus the messages since. Nightleaf's runs every 20 messages.
The model call that writes a summary. Nightleaf's reads the old summary and the newest messages, and writes the next summary.
The messages a summariser reads in one pass: here, the 20 messages since the last summary.
One run of the summariser, which turns the old summary and one batch into a new summary.
A summary written from an earlier summary plus newer text, again and again. MemGPT's term. Each pass can lose detail the last pass dropped.
Here, a summary moving away from what was said, a little at each rewrite, because each rewrite starts from the last summary.
This case's word for a summariser making two entries into one to save space, as Nightleaf's did with the two sisters.
One short thing worth remembering, such as a sister's new town. Nightleaf's summaries are lists of facts by person.
A fact stored with the date it was said and the message it came from, so it can be checked, ordered and deleted with its source.
The message a fact was taken from. Storing it with the fact is what lets a delete find every copy.
A model call that pulls facts from a new message while the conversation is still in the window, and stores each with its date and source.
Where dated facts are kept: a table or index the app searches each night for the facts that matter.
Long-term memory kept outside the model and fetched into the window only when relevant, the way retrieval fetches passages in Season 3.
A word the sim tags a fact or an entry with, such as rang or lonely. The sim fetches the facts sharing the most topics with tonight's entry.
The most tokens an app lets itself send on one call, set to control cost. Nightleaf's is 600 a night, a teaching value far below the model's window.
The sim's teaching value for the model's context window: 200,000 tokens, more than a year of Lowenna's diary at September's rate.
The sim's rule-following replacement for a real summarising model. It shows the mechanism and measures no real model.
The sim's rule-following replacement for the model that writes Nightleaf's reply on night 31.
Nightleaf's delete button. It removed the stored message and nothing derived from it.
Here, anything holding a piece of the original: the message, a summary line written from it, a fact, a backup or a log.
A 2023 research system by Packer and colleagues that manages an assistant's memory in tiers, inside and outside the context window.
MemGPT's idea, after operating systems: move information between the context window and outside storage so the model seems to have more memory.
MemGPT's part that keeps recent messages in the window and, when it fills, evicts some and writes a new recursive summary.
To move something out of the context window to make room. MemGPT evicts older messages from its queue.
MemGPT's store of every message, outside the window, searchable by the model. Evicted messages are kept there.
Keeping less than the original, so some detail can't be got back. A summary is lossy.
A search that returns results a page at a time, so a large result never floods the window.
The software that runs a computer and moves data between fast, small memory and slow, large storage.
A tool Claude can call to create, read, update and delete files in a memory directory. Your application stores the files and runs each operation.
Run by your application, not the provider. The memory tool's files live in storage you control.
Deleting personal data so it is gone. GDPR Article 17 calls the right to it the right to erasure.
In GDPR, the organisation that decides why and how personal data is processed. Here, Idris's company.
In GDPR, the person the personal data is about. Here, Lowenna, and her sisters in what she writes.
GDPR's phrase for as soon as reasonably possible, with no needless wait.
The GDPR principle in Article 5(1)(e): keep personal data in a form that identifies people no longer than the purpose needs.
Keeping data for a period. A retention rule says how long, and when it must be deleted.
A model-based assistant that answers customers for a company, often with memory of each customer's past contacts.
A customer's formal report of a problem, opened, worked on and closed by a support team.
Replaced by something newer. A fact superseded by a newer one about the same thing should no longer be sent as true.
A room or unit of beds in a hospital, with its own nurses.
A trial period at the start of a new job, after which the employer confirms the post.
A school holiday of about a week in the middle of each term in the UK, often used for visits.
A shop that sells donated goods to raise money for a charity.
One request to a model and its answer. Nightleaf makes one a night for the reply, and its summariser is another.
Large language model. MemGPT's paper uses the short form.
To train an existing model further on new examples so its weights change. It is not how an assistant remembers one user.
Singapore's Data Protection Trustmark, a certification that an organisation's personal data practices meet the PDPA and related standards.
A new version of an app shipped to its users.

atWork: Find an assistant at work that remembers people across conversations: a customer-service bot with each customer's history, a sales assistant with notes on accounts, an internal helper that knows your preferences. A common incident: a customer-service bot kept a rolling summary per customer, and a complaint that had been closed in its third message came back as open in the summary's next rewrite, so the bot apologised for it to the customer for weeks. Ask four things. Is its memory written from the original messages or from earlier summaries? Does each remembered item keep its date and the message it came from? What does it send each call, and how does that grow with a long-time customer? And when someone asks it to forget something, which copies does the delete reach: the message, the summary, the index, the backups, the logs? Standards-readiness note: if the memories hold personal data and GDPR applies, Article 17 gives people the right to erasure without undue delay, and Article 5(1)(e) limits how long data that identifies them is kept; design deletes that follow the source to every copy, and a retention rule for unused memories, from the first version. If your organisation holds or seeks DPTM in Singapore, the PDPA's retention limitation obligation asks the same of you.

recall.prompt: Your support assistant keeps one rolling summary per customer, rewritten every 30 messages from the previous summary and the new messages. A customer with a personal account and a business account is told her business invoice is overdue on her personal account. A card number she asked support to forget last month still shows up in the assistant's replies, although the message holding it was deleted. What is going on, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Each summary is written from the last summary, not the original messages, so which account a message meant gets lost and two get mixed: summaries of summaries drift
The summary is a copy of the deleted message with no link back to it, so the delete never reached it
Keep memory as dated facts with their source message, fetch the relevant ones, and let the customer see and delete them

recall.model: Her memory is a rolling summary, and each version is written from the last summary plus the newest messages, never from the originals. Whatever an earlier pass dropped, such as which account a message was about, is gone for good, so a later pass files the invoice under the account the summary says more about: summaries of summaries drift. The card number is the same problem from the other side. The delete removed the message, but a summary had already copied it, and that copy has no link back to its source, so nothing found it. I would keep memory as dated facts, each written once from the original conversation with its date and its source message and the account it belongs to, fetch only the relevant facts each turn, and let the customer see and delete them. Deleting a message then deletes every fact that points to it, and the old summaries go.

recall.prompt: In MemGPT (Packer and colleagues, 2023), what happens when the queue of recent messages fills the context window?
options: The oldest messages are deleted, and nothing about them is kept
Some messages are evicted, a new recursive summary is written from the existing summary and the evicted messages, and the evicted messages are kept in recall storage
The whole conversation is sent again in a larger context window
The model is fine-tuned on the evicted messages so it remembers them
recall.why: The paper's queue manager evicts a specific count of messages and generates a new recursive summary using the existing recursive summary and evicted messages. The evicted messages leave the window but are stored indefinitely in recall storage, where the model can search them. So MemGPT does not rely on the summary alone: the originals are kept and can be brought back.

recall.prompt: A user of your journaling assistant asks you to delete everything she wrote about a former partner. Your app stores her messages, a nightly rolling summary written from the previous one, a search index of her messages, and nightly backups kept for 30 days. Your delete button removes messages. What does a real delete need, and what would you change so the next one is easy?

keyIdeas.idea: Every copy has to go: the messages, the summary, the search index and the backups, not just the message rows
Derived items need a pointer back to their source message so the delete can find them; a summary has none
Let her see what is kept and confirm it is gone; keep memories no longer than needed

recall.model: Deleting the message rows isn't enough, because every copy has to go: the messages, the lines of the rolling summary written from them, the entries in the search index, and the backups, which can be left to expire on their 30-day schedule if she is told so. The summary is the hard part. It is written from the previous summary and has no record of which message each sentence came from, so you can't find what to remove; you have to rebuild it from the originals, or better, stop keeping memory that way. Store memories as dated facts with a pointer to their source message, and index entries the same way, so a delete follows the source to everything built from it. Show her the list of what is kept, confirm when it's gone, and expire memories nobody has used for a long time. Where GDPR applies this is the right to erasure, without undue delay.

recall.prompt: With Nightleaf sending her whole history every night, night 31 cost 997 tokens. September's 60 messages came to 977 tokens. At that rate, about how many tokens would one night cost a year after she started?
options: About 997, because the history is only sent once
About 11,922, because every night adds about 33 tokens that are sent again every night after
recall.why: Each night adds her entry and the reply, about 977 / 30, roughly 33 tokens, and whole history sends all of them again every night. After 365 nights that is 35 for the system prompt plus 977 x 365 / 30, about 11,887, so about 11,922 tokens a night, and the total over the year grows faster still, because every night pays for all the nights before it.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. Idris shipped dated facts in October, and Nightleaf has asked after the right sister ever since. I read my fact list most Sundays. On 9 January I wrote that Tegwen had left the hospital job and moved back to town, two streets from me, and the list shows it: "Tegwen: moved back home, 9 Jan". On 20 January I wrote "My sister rang, she's lonely again", and Nightleaf asked how she was getting on in Carrowmere. Both facts are in the list. The September one about Carrowmere being lonely in the evenings is still there too.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did Nightleaf ask about Carrowmere, and what should Idris change?

keyIdeas.idea: The old Carrowmere fact matched more of the night's words (rang, lonely) than the January one, so retrieval fetched it and the reply used it
Nothing marks the old fact as replaced: a newer fact about the same thing should supersede or retire the older one
Use the dates: prefer the newest fact about a person's place, check for conflicts when writing, and let her fix it

coldCase.model: The facts were right; the choice between them was wrong. The night's entry shared rang and lonely with September's "Carrowmere is lonely in the evenings", and only sister with January's "moved back home", so retrieval ranked the old fact higher and the reply asked about Carrowmere. Nothing in the store said the September facts about where Tegwen lives were out of date. The fix is in how facts are written: when a new fact is about the same thing as an old one, such as where Tegwen lives, the writer should supersede the old one, keeping it with its date as history but marking it no longer true, so it isn't sent as current. Retrieval should then prefer the newest fact about each person and thing, which is what the dates are for. When the writer finds a conflict it can't settle, it can ask her or show both in the list, where she can fix it.

Liu, Kevin Lin, John Hewitt, Ashwin Paranjape, Michele Bevilacqua, Fabio Petroni, Percy Liang, Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts, arXiv 2307.03172 (2023): performance is often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context, and significantly degrades when models must access relevant information in the middle of long contexts, even for explicitly long-context models
